problem: End-to-end whole-body VLAs such as π0.5-based openpi-comet do poorly on long-horizon mobile manipulation in BEHAVIOR-1K; the best 2025 challenge entry reaches only 12.4% success. They fail even though they are fine-tuned on 1,200 h of teleoperation data. Prior VLA + motion-planner hybrids only handle short pre-grasp motions with fixed-base VLAs on short pick-and-place tasks, or, like AnywhereVLA, detect no subtask completion and do no task decomposition.
motivation: A failure analysis of top BEHAVIOR-1K solutions (Rasouli et al.) found recurring failures: navigation failures, collisions, execution-order confusion and abrupt termination. The baseline fails even on evaluation episodes that lie inside the dense support of the training trajectories, which suggests more data will not fix it. Classical planning is designed to handle exactly these failure modes: reaching distant or occluded objects and finding collision-free paths through clutter.
key_idea: Interleave a classical navigation stack (A* + pure pursuit, GroundingDINO detection, frontier exploration) with an off-the-shelf VLA used only for manipulation near the target. An LLM subtask plan drives the switching, and VLM completion checks are gated by proprioceptive triggers.
insight: Most of the gain comes from classical navigation plus reliable handoffs, not from decomposition or perception alone. On the 12-task ablation subset: (1) giving the VLA the same subtask decomposition without the motion planner is 41% better than the baseline but 31% worse than MPVI. (2) Replacing proprioception-triggered VLM checks with 10 s periodic polling cuts performance by 47%. Periodic polling produces false positives that cascade, and false negatives that leave the robot stuck in the VLA. (3) Oracle object positions add only 17%, mostly on large open outdoor tasks such as hiding_Easter_eggs, so perception and exploration are not the main bottleneck. On 20 episode pairs with matched Q-scores, efficiency is similar: 4.5% less base distance and 9.8% less normalized sim time. The benefit is therefore robustness, not navigation efficiency. The approach regresses where the VLA navigates better than the planner, e.g. narrow doorways while carrying objects.
method: Subtask Planner: an LLM fine-tuned on human-annotated BEHAVIOR-1K task plans. It turns the instruction into ordered segments (type ∈ {navigation, manipulation}, description, nav target, state-based completion criterion). Post-processing maps manipulation segments to pick/place primitives and flags segments that immediately precede a navigation segment.

Orchestrator: dispatches navigation segments one at a time and groups consecutive manipulation segments into one VLA unit, which uses the final segment's completion criterion. It keeps a knowledge base of rooms, areas, fixtures and discovered object locations so later navigation can reuse them, and marks a subtask failed and advances when a time budget runs out.

Navigation: A* on an a-priori traversability map with labeled rooms plus a pure-pursuit base controller, with arms held fixed. The target is found via the knowledge base; otherwise the robot goes to the named room, runs GroundingDINO on the head camera, and back-projects the box center using median depth. If nothing is detected it does frontier exploration with ray-based visibility maps. Navigation ends within handoff distance d_h of the target.

Manipulation: openpi-comet (π0.5 fine-tuned on BEHAVIOR challenge teleop data, MP-synthesized trajectories and RL rollouts), used without further training. It gets the subtask text plus head and wrist RGB and outputs whole-body actions, including base repositioning inside d_h.

Completion Checker: Gemini 2.5 Flash gives a binary YES/NO on a state-based criterion from a camera image. It is only queried when proprioceptive heuristics fire, e.g. gripper closed at nonzero width for a grasp, or object release for a place. Only the terminal state before a navigation segment is verified. If not confirmed, the VLA continues until timeout.

setting.action_space: base: A* path tracked by pure-pursuit controller (continuous base motion); manipulation: VLA low-level whole-body robot actions

Task object locations are not given, except in the 'Oracle Object Localization' ablation, which uses GT simulator object positions.

numbers_note: No success rate and no absolute mean Q-score are printed. Aggregate results appear only as relative percentages in figure captions and text, and the summary figures themselves are not in the text. The appendix gives per-task Q-scores for all 50 tasks (MPVI vs. E2E VLA), e.g. collecting_childrens_toys 0.00→0.56, bringing_water 0.23→0.70, picking_up_trash 0.63→0.90, loading_the_car 0.30→0.00. It also gives per-task Q-scores for all ablation variants on the 12-task subset. This is a mobile-manipulation benchmark (Q-score = fraction of BDDL goal predicates satisfied), not a navigation benchmark.
results: On all 50 BEHAVIOR-1K challenge tasks, MPVI raises mean Q-score by 113% over the re-run openpi-comet baseline (2nd place, whole-body π0.5), with no extra data or VLA training. It improves 31 tasks, ties 16 and regresses on 3: loading_the_car 0.30→0.00, moving_boxes_to_storage 0.80→0.56, set_up_a_coffee_station 0.20→0.15. Gains concentrate on long-horizon, multi-location tasks. Tasks bottlenecked by dexterous manipulation (e.g. attach_a_camera_to_a_tripod) stay at 0.
limitations: Requires a pre-mapped traversability map with labeled rooms and fixtures plus accurate localization, so it cannot be deployed in unmapped environments.

Classical planning is used only for navigation, so there is no gain on dexterous-manipulation-bound tasks. The static navigation/manipulation boundary can override the VLA where it does better (e.g. narrow doorways while carrying objects), causing regressions.
Evaluation is simulation only (OmniGibson), and only against one baseline re-run in the authors' own framework. Only Q-score and relative aggregates are reported, with no success rate.
